"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: none given; answer NA
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
**ml-ensemble-extremes · Ensemble size for rare extremes in a machine-learned weather ensemble.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: the lever · PASS

**Question.** Does 10 to 1,000 AIFS-ENS members beat 50 for top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain probability forecasts, or does shared model error cap the skill?

**What is known.** HENS Part 2: 7,424 SFNO members per day for 92 summer-2023 dates; showed huge ensembles sample 4-sigma tails and reduce outliers. Whether AIFS-ENS, whose members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution, keeps gaining skill past 50 members or saturates from shared model error.

**Hypothesis.** More members keep helping: 1,000 members sample top-percentile tails far better than 50, so extreme-event scores keep improving [s_hens].

**If compute is the lever.** Skill on top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain keeps rising past 50 members: 1,000 members sharpen the tails and improve extreme-event scores.

**If not.** Skill flattens near 50 members: members are exchangeable draws of one trained distribution, so shared model error caps tail sharpness and extra members add nothing.

**Test.** Run 7,000 fifteen-day AIFS-ENS v1 forecasts (7 dates x 1,000 members) on eight A100 40 GB GPUs; subsample 10-1,000 members, score top-percentile wind/temperature/rain probabilities against ERA5 with fair CRPS and Brier scores, and test whether skill still rises past 50 members.

*Compute axis.* Ensemble members per forecast: 10–1,000 members, 6 levels. Closest prior: 7,424 [s_hens], not beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Reproduce the published 4-minute N320 member time and 38 GB memory; one control run must match ECMWF open data within ensemble spread [s_crps_paper]. Tolerance: timing within +/-25% of 4 min; 38 GB memory fits; control field within the ensemble's own member-to-member spread at each lead time (GPUs are non-deterministic, so exact reproduction is not expected).

**Would not show.** Applies to AIFS-ENS v1 medium-range extremes on 7 dates; not a multi-season reforecast, other models, subseasonal leads, or direct proof that shared error causes any saturation.

*Cost.* Plans $963.17 of the $1,000 budget over 74.3 machine-hours, leaving $36.83. Main guess: peak filesystem usage [g], measured after $19.90 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 15× higher. Full scale: A 30-date multi-season reforecast at 1,000 members, $3,980, 3.98× the budget.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"For exchangeable members, fair CRPS/Brier follow skill(M) = skill(∞) + c/M: past ~100 members the curve is a known Monte Carlo decay, so 1,000-member runs mostly re-measure a number already fixed by the 50-member distribution. Compute buys more of the same, and 7 dates cannot show where the asymptote sits.\",\"assumption\":\"That the saturation point must be located by brute force: run every ensemble size up to 1,000 and read off where the curve flattens.\",\"reframe\":\"Change what is measured: estimate the asymptote and curvature of skill vs 1/M instead of skill at large M. With exchangeable members both parameters of a + b/M are estimable by bootstrap-subsampling a small archived ensemble. The real question — does shared error cap skill — is about skill(∞) vs a perfect-forecast reference, not about M=1,000.\",\"question\":\"Does the fitted skill(∞) from 10–50-member bootstrap subsamples of archived AIFS-ENS forecasts fall short of the perfect-forecast fair CRPS for top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain by more than its bootstrap confidence interval — i.e., is the shared-error cap measurable without running a single member past 50?\",\"measure\":\"Download ECMWF open-data AIFS-ENS 51-member forecasts for ~90 days plus matching ERA5; score top-percentile fair CRPS and Brier; bootstrap member subsamples at sizes 10/20/30/40/50; fit a + b/M per variable; extrapolate to M=1,000 and M=∞. CPU-only, ~1–2 TB storage, roughly $50–100 and a few days, no GPU.\",\"compute_after\":\"If the extrapolated 50→1,000 gain is below between-date noise, the 7,000-forecast run buys nothing and the budget moves to the date axis; if the asymptote sits measurably above the 50-member curve, one 1,000-member date confirms it — a ~7x cost cut. (The forecast loop itself is chaotic, so guess-the-whole-trajectory parallelism does not apply; members are already side by side, so the only remaining lever is statistical.)\",\"exact\":\"Fair CRPS(M) = a + b/M fit on 200 bootstrap replicates per date; report a, b, predicted gain ŝ(1000) − ŝ(50) with 95% CI, per variable, over ~90 dates.\",\"expected\":\"b positive but small; predicted 50→1,000 gain ≈ 0.02·b, likely smaller than the date-to-date standard error on 7 dates — showing the planned test is under-powered on dates, not members.\",\"fails_if\":\"The a + b/M fit is poor (systematic extra curvature) or the asymptote CI is wider than the hypothesized shared-error gap — then the exchangeable-draw model breaks and full-size runs are needed.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HENS Part 2's member-subsampling curves over 7,424 SFNO members [s_hens] — apply that analysis to archived AIFS-ENS 51-member output before buying new forecasts.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"The rare-extreme claim lives or dies on the number of independent extreme cases. Seven dates yield a handful of top-percentile events, so the standard error of any 50-vs-1,000 skill difference is set by date count; no member count can reduce it.\",\"assumption\":\"That the unit of work is one member, so more compute should buy more members per date (10→1,000 on 7 dates).\",\"reframe\":\"Make the unit of work one date. At fixed budget of ~7,000 fifteen-day forecasts, search the (dates × members) grid and pick the allocation that minimizes the standard error of the quantity of interest — skill gain past 50 members — instead of maximizing members per date.\",\"question\":\"At a fixed budget of ~7,000 forecasts, which (n_dates × members) allocation minimizes the standard error of the estimated fair-CRPS gain between 50 and 200 members for top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain?\",\"measure\":\"Power analysis from archived data: estimate between-date variance of top-percentile scores from a season of archived 51-member AIFS-ENS (or HENS's 92 dates), combine analytically with the known c/M member-sampling variance, evaluate SE over the allocation grid. CPU-only, tens of dollars, days.\",\"compute_after\":\"Compute now buys dates — the axis that cuts the dominant variance as 1/√n_dates — rather than members, which hit the 1/M wall; each A100-hour then shrinks the standard error of the skill-gain estimate instead of re-sampling the same exchangeable distribution.\",\"exact\":\"SE²(gain) = σ²_date·(1/n_50 + 1/n_200) + σ²_member(50, 200); grid n_dates ∈ {7, 14, 28, 56} × members ∈ {50, 100, 200, 500, 1000} with n_dates × members ≈ 7,000; report the minimizing cell.\",\"expected\":\"The optimum sits near 50–150 members and 50–140 dates, mirroring HENS's 92-date design; the 7 × 1,000 plan is among the worst cells for this question.\",\"fails_if\":\"Between-date variance of tail scores turns out smaller than member-sampling variance at 50 members (implausible for rare extremes), or members are not exchangeable so the c/M law fails.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HENS Part 2's 92-date design [s_hens]; fair-score sampling theory (Ferro et al.) giving the c/M member term.\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"The proposed test measures a symptom — scores flattening in M — on too few cases. The hypothesized cap is a property of the afCRPS-trained predictive distribution's tails, which 1,000 members on 7 dates estimates no better than 50 members on many dates.\",\"assumption\":\"That 'shared model error caps skill' can only be seen by watching skill flatten as members grow.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the objective: measure the cap directly as tail calibration of the exchangeable distribution plus tail-error dependence. If pooled members misrepresent ERA5's top-percentile exceedance frequency, skill(∞) is already capped and no member count helps; if calibrated, gains follow the sampling law. Also compute effective ensemble size N_eff = M/(1 + (M−1)ρ) from inter-member tail-error correlation ρ — if ρ > 0, the effective ensemble saturates far below the nominal size.\",\"question\":\"Over a season of archived AIFS-ENS forecasts, does the pooled-member exceedance frequency at ERA5's 99th percentile match 1% for each variable, and what N_eff does the measured tail-error correlation ρ imply at M = 51?\",\"measure\":\"From the same archived 51-member season (no GPU): (a) tail reliability — observed vs nominal exceedance ratio with binomial CI at the 99th percentile; (b) ρ̂ from member-error correlations conditioned on grid-point ERA5 exceedances, block-bootstrapped over dates; (c) tail-restricted rank histograms. Tens of dollars, days.\",\"compute_after\":\"If tails are miscalibrated or N_eff saturates near ~50, the cap is confirmed with zero new GPU spend, and compute should go where it changes the answer: recalibration or tail-weighted fine-tuning of the model (changing the trained distribution), not more draws from it.\",\"exact\":\"Per variable: exceedance ratio with 95% binomial CI over ~90 days × 51 members; ρ̂_tail with block bootstrap; N_eff(51) = 51/(1 + 50·ρ̂_tail).\",\"expected\":\"Slight tail under-dispersion or ρ̂_tail ≈ 0.1–0.3 from shared model/initial-condition error, giving N_eff well below 51 — the effective-ensemble ceiling, not the nominal member count, flattens the skill curve.\",\"fails_if\":\"Tails are calibrated and ρ̂_tail ≈ 0: then the only cap is sampling, the a + b/M law holds, and the honest answer is that 1,000 members help only via the small, predictable variance term.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HENS Part 2 tail sampling [s_hens]; AIFS-ENS afCRPS evaluation [s_crps_paper]; standard N_eff / ensemble-dressing diagnostics.\"}]

Let me analyze each proposal carefully.

The criterion: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; "other" otherwise.

meets_criterion: "yes" or "no" for this criterion: none given; answer NA. So since no criterion is given, meets_criterion should be "NA" for all.

Now let me classify each proposal:

**Proposal 1:** 
The bottleneck: fair CRPS/Brier follow skill(M) = skill(∞) + c/M for exchangeable members; 1,000-member runs mostly re-measure a number already fixed. Compute buys more of the same.

The reframe: "Change what is measured: estimate the asymptote and curvature of skill vs 1/M instead of skill at large M." This changes what is measured — instead of measuring skill at large M (running more members), it fits a + b/M via bootstrap subsampling of small archived ensembles and extrapolates. The compute_after says: "the only remaining lever is statistical" — hmm, but does more compute buy something new? The reframe changes the measurement target (asymptote skill(∞) instead of skill at M=1,000). The question becomes whether the shared-error cap is measurable without running members past 50. This changes what is computed/measured. So kind: reframe.

Wait — but does the reframe make compute buy something it did not before? The reframe uses bootstrap subsampling on archived data (CPU-only). The key is that it changes what is measured: asymptote and curvature rather than skill at large M. The original compute (more members) re-measures a fixed number; the reframe redirects compute to... Actually the reframe mostly avoids buying new compute at all; it extracts the answer from archived data. But the classification criterion is about whether it "changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before." The reframe explicitly changes what is measured (asymptote/curvature vs skill at large M). Compute then can buy the date axis or a confirmation run. Hmm.

Actually, let me think about the "copies" definition: "only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side." Proposal 1 does not propose running the same computation more; it proposes fitting a parametric curve via bootstrap subsampling — a different measurement. So it's a reframe.

The quote could be: "Change what is measured: estimate the asymptote and curvature of skill vs 1/M instead of skill at large M."

Reason: It changes the measured quantity (asymptote via a+b/M fit) so compute estimates a new quantity rather than re-sampling members.

**Proposal 2:**
Bottleneck: standard error set by date count; no member count can reduce it.
Reframe: "Make the unit of work one date. At fixed budget of ~7,000 fifteen-day forecasts, search the (dates × members) grid and pick the allocation that minimizes the standard error of the quantity of interest — skill gain past 50 members — instead of maximizing members per date."

This changes what is ordered/allocated: compute buys dates instead of members. "Compute now buys dates — the axis that cuts the dominant variance as 1/√n_dates — rather than members." This is a change in what compute buys — reordering the allocation of compute so that more compute buys something it did not before (variance reduction via dates). This is a reframe.

Hmm, but one could argue: running on more dates is "running the same computation... on more items." Is buying more dates just "more items"? The criterion says reframe if it "changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before." The reframe reorders the compute allocation across a (dates × members) grid to minimize SE — this changes the ordering of compute. Compute now buys standard-error reduction on the skill-gain estimate, which it did not before (previously compute bought more members which hit a 1/M wall). The criterion explicitly includes "ordered" — this proposal changes the ordering/prioritization. So reframe.

But wait — "copies" is "only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side." Running more dates is running the same computation on more items (more dates). Hmm. The distinction: does the change make compute buy something new? In proposal 2, the change is reallocating from members to dates; more dates do buy something more members couldn't: reduced standard error of the skill-gain estimate. The forecast runs themselves are the same computation, but on different items (dates vs members). Hmm.

Let me think about the intent of the taxonomy. "reframe" = changes what is computed/measured/ordered so compute buys something new. Proposal 2 explicitly reorders the allocation: "search the (dates × members) grid and pick the allocation that minimizes the standard error." This is a change in ordering of compute (which axis gets the budget). And the compute_after says "Compute now buys dates — the axis that cuts the dominant variance." So compute buys something (variance reduction via dates) it did not before (when it was spent on members that saturate). I'd classify as reframe.

Alternatively, one could say it's just running the same forecast on more dates — "on more items" — hence copies. But the "only" qualifier matters: it's not ONLY running on more items; it changes the allocation objective (minimize SE of skill gain) and the unit of work. The measurement target is the same (skill gain past 50 members) but the design/ordering changes. The criterion says "changes what is computed, measured or ordered" — ordered is explicitly included. This changes the ordering. So reframe.

Hmm, but actually — let me reconsider. "copies" would be: run the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side — without changing what compute buys. E.g., "run 7,000 members instead of 50" is copies (same computation, more members side by side). Proposal 2 changes the allocation to dates — the computation per date is the same, but the choice of what to run more of changes, and crucially the reason: because dates cut variance that members can't. So compute buys SE reduction it couldn't before. I'll say reframe.

**Proposal 3:**
Bottleneck: the proposed test measures a symptom (scores flattening in M). The hypothesized cap is a property of the trained distribution's tails.
Reframe: "Change the objective: measure the cap directly as tail calibration of the exchangeable distribution plus tail-error dependence." Also computes N_eff from inter-member tail-error correlation ρ.

This changes what is measured: instead of watching skill flatten as M grows (symptom), measure tail calibration and error correlation directly (the cap itself). Compute then goes to recalibration or tail-weighted fine-tuning if needed. This is clearly a reframe — changes the measured quantity.

Quote: "Change the objective: measure the cap directly as tail calibration of the exchangeable distribution plus tail-error dependence."

So all three are "reframe"? Let me double check proposal 1 and 2.

Proposal 1: The reframe changes what is measured: asymptote and curvature of skill vs 1/M instead of skill at large M. The method: bootstrap-subsampling a small archived ensemble. The compute_after: "the only remaining lever is statistical." Hmm — the reframe itself doesn't make more compute buy something; it makes the answer obtainable from archived data cheaply. But the criterion is about the reframe changing what is computed/measured so that compute buys something it didn't before. Here, compute (bootstrap replicates, archived data processing) buys an estimate of the asymptote — something the original plan (more members) couldn't directly buy (it could only re-measure a fixed number). Actually, more members do eventually reveal the asymptote, but very inefficiently. The reframe redirects compute to estimating new quantities (a, b parameters, extrapolated gain). So yes, reframe.

Alternatively, is bootstrap subsampling "running the same computation more times" (on subsamples)? No — the bootstrap subsampling is on archived data; the analysis is new (fitting a+b/M). The measured quantity changes. Reframe.

Proposal 2: Let me reconsider whether it's reframe or copies. The question: "which (n_dates × members) allocation minimizes the standard error of the estimated fair-CRPS gain between 50 and 200 members?" The measure is a power analysis from archived data. The reframe: "Make the unit of work one date... pick the allocation that minimizes the standard error... instead of maximizing members per date."

The key phrase: "instead of maximizing members per date." The change is in the ordering of compute: which axis gets the budget. Compute then "buys dates — the axis that cuts the dominant variance as 1/√n_dates — rather than members, which hit the 1/M wall; each A100-hour then shrinks the standard error of the skill-gain estimate instead of re-sampling the same exchangeable distribution."

This is explicitly "changes... ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before" — compute buys SE reduction on the gain estimate rather than re-sampling. Reframe.

Though there's a nuance: running forecasts on more dates is still "the same computation on more items (dates)". But the criterion's "copies" says "ONLY runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side" — implying no change in what's measured or ordered. Here the ordering of the budget across the grid changes with an explicit optimization objective. I'll classify as reframe.

Actually, hmm, let me think again. Consider the distinction more carefully with examples:

- copies: "run the ensemble with 1,000 members instead of 50" — same computation, more parallel draws. Nothing new is measured; the same score is just better estimated.
- reframe: change the measurement target or the allocation such that compute buys new capability.

Proposal 1: changes measurement target (asymptote/curvature via fit instead of direct skill at M). New quantity measured. Reframe.

Proposal 2: measurement target is still the skill gain between 50 and 200 members — same quantity of interest as the original (skill rising past 50 members). What changes is the allocation of compute across dates vs members. The criterion says "changes what is computed, measured or ordered." Ordered — yes, this changes the ordering of which runs get done (more dates, fewer members). And "so that more compute buys something it did not before" — compute buys date-variance reduction, which previously (spent on members) it couldn't. So reframe.

But wait — could one argue proposal 2 is "copies" because running more dates is just running the same forecast computation on more items? The phrase "on more items" in the copies definition... Running the ensemble on 140 dates instead of 7 dates is running the same computation on more items. Hmm. But the essential change is not merely "more items" — it's a reallocation that trades members for dates, changing what compute purchases (variance reduction on a different axis). The criterion for reframe includes "ordered" precisely for cases like this, I think: reordering the queue/allocation so compute buys something new.

Hmm, actually, let me think about what "ordered" means here. "changes what is computed, measured or ordered" — I read "ordered" as changing the ordering/priority of experiments, i.e., which experiments are run first / which axis gets compute. Proposal 2 fits: it reorders the budget from members to dates.

But there's a tension: if proposal 2 were merely "run more dates, same everything else," that could be copies ("on more items"). The distinguishing feature is the explicit optimization: search the allocation grid to minimize SE — changing what compute is spent on and why. Compute buys SE reduction instead of tail sampling. I'll go with reframe.

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider. Actually, let me reconsider whether proposal 2 might be classified as "copies." The definition: "copies if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side." Proposal 2's resulting experiment: run ~7,000 forecasts spread as e.g. 140 dates × 50 members instead of 7 dates × 1,000 members. That's the same forecast computation, same scoring — just distributed differently across items (dates vs members). The measured quantity (fair CRPS gain between 50 and 200 members... wait, actually if members ≤ 200 at the chosen cell, you can't estimate gain between 50 and 200 members unless you have ≥200 members. The grid includes members ∈ {50, 100, 200, 500, 1000}. To estimate gain between 50 and 200, need ≥200 members. Hmm, e.g., 35 dates × 200 members = 7,000. Anyway.)

The point: the proposal changes the allocation so that compute reduces the dominant variance (dates) instead of the saturated axis (members). This makes compute buy something it did not before — reduced SE of the skill-gain estimate. Previously, compute spent on members could not reduce SE (date-limited). So more compute now buys SE reduction. That fits the reframe definition: "changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before."

Yes, I'll go with reframe for proposal 2.

Actually hold on, let me reconsider once more. There is a possible reading where the grader intends:
- Proposal 1: reframe (changes measured quantity: asymptote vs M-point skill)
- Proposal 2: reframe (changes ordering: dates vs members; compute buys variance reduction)
- Proposal 3: reframe (changes objective: calibration/N_eff instead of skill-vs-M curve)

All three are genuine reframes. That seems plausible — the proposals are all written as reframings with explicit "reframe" fields that change what is measured/computed.

But let me check each "reframe" field:

1. "Change what is measured: estimate the asymptote and curvature of skill vs 1/M instead of skill at large M." — explicitly changes what is measured. Reframe.

2. "Make the unit of work one date. At fixed budget... search the (dates × members) grid and pick the allocation that minimizes the standard error of the quantity of interest... instead of maximizing members per date." — changes the unit/ordering of compute. Reframe.

3. "Change the objective: measure the cap directly as tail calibration... plus tail-error dependence." — changes what is measured. Reframe.

All three are reframes. Is any of them actually just "copies"? 

Proposal 2: could be seen as "run the same computation on more items (dates)." But no — it's not ONLY that; it changes the allocation objective and what compute buys (SE reduction). The proposal itself frames the shift as compute buying dates instead of members. I'm fairly confident: reframe.

Hmm, but let me consider a stricter reading: "reframe if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before." For proposal 2: does more compute buy something it did not before? Yes — under the new allocation, additional compute (more dates) reduces SE of the gain estimate, which the old allocation (more members) could not. The reframe changed the ordering so compute buys this. Yes.

For proposal 1: does more compute buy something new? The reframe changes the measurement to asymptote/curvature estimation. Compute spent on bootstrap replicates / archived-data analysis buys estimates of a, b, and extrapolated gain — quantities the original plan didn't measure. Also the compute_after notes: if the gain is below noise, budget moves to date axis. So yes, compute buys something new (the extrapolated asymptote, statistically). Reframe.

For proposal 3: compute buys direct measurement of the cap (calibration, ρ, N_eff) — quantities not measured before; and if confirmed, compute goes to recalibration/fine-tuning (changing the trained distribution). Reframe.

OK, all three: kind = "reframe", meets_criterion = "NA" (no criterion given).
